title: Where your program starts (Main and top-level statements)
hook: Every executable program needs exactly one starting point. In C# you either write a classic static Main method or put statements at the top of one file and let the compiler build Main for you.

blocks.text: The entry point is the method the operating system calls when your process starts. In classic C# you write static void Main(string[] args) or static int Main to return an exit code. Modern templates use top-level statements: plain executable lines at the top of a single file. The compiler silently generates a Program class and a Main-like method. Both styles produce the same kind of executable — top-level statements are syntactic sugar, not a different runtime.

entries.plainDefinition: The static method the CLR calls first when your executable starts.
Executable C# lines written outside any class; the compiler synthesizes an entry point from them.
entries.example: Console.WriteLine("hello"); as the entire Program.cs file body.

entries.plainDefinition: A string array of values passed to your program when it is launched.
entries.example: dotnet run -- queue-name passes "queue-name" into args[0].

blocks.text: Only one file per compilation may contain top-level statements. If you copy Program.cs and leave top-level code in both, the build fails. Worker hosts (generic host, AWS Lambda handlers) often hide Main inside the framework — your "entry" becomes a handler method, but the process still started at Main under the hood. Understanding args, return codes, and async entry points prevents subtle bugs in command-line tools and services.

blocks.title: One entry per executable
blocks.body: Exactly one entry point per executable compilation. Two files with top-level statements will not compile together.

items.title: OS launches the process
items.body: The runtime loader finds the assembly and locates the entry point metadata.

items.title: CLR calls Main (or synthesized Main)
items.body: Top-level statements compile to a hidden static Main method in a generated Program class.

items.title: args arrives as string[]
items.body: Command-line tokens are available in the args parameter or as a top-level args variable.

items.title: Return code becomes exit code
items.body: return 0 from Main (or top-level return 0) tells the OS the program succeeded.

diagram.title: Entry point styles

flowchart TD
  A[Process starts] --> B{Entry style}

  B -->|Top-level| D[Compiler-generated Main]
  C --> E[Your application code]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Exit code to OS]

snippet.label: Top-level statements (default template)
snippet.explanation: args is in scope automatically. No class or Main wrapper needed. The compiler generates the entry point behind the scenes.

snippet.label: Equivalent explicit Main
snippet.explanation: Return codes from Main become the process exit code. Top-level return of an int does the same. Both styles are fully equivalent.

snippet.label: Async entry with await at top level
snippet.explanation: Top-level await changes the generated signature to async Task Main. Useful for console tools that call APIs without blocking.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Two Program.cs files both with top-level statements after a copy-paste. Looking for Main in a new template and concluding the app has no entry point. Forgetting that await at top-level changes the synthesized signature to async Main.

interviewTakeaways: Exactly one entry point per executable compilation.
Top-level statements are syntactic sugar for a synthesized Main, not a different runtime model.
`args` is the process argument vector, same idea as `process.argv.slice(2)` but typed as `string[]`.
commonPitfalls: Two Program.cs files both with top-level statements after a copy-paste.
Looking for `Main` in a new template and concluding the app has no entry point.
Forgetting that `await` at top-level changes the synthesized signature to async Main.
